findings.headline: External net debt to grow 39% from £396.0m to £551.7m—material increase in leverage
findings.detail: The council's net external debt is projected to rise from £396.0m to £551.7m over the forecast period as capital programs are funded predominantly through new borrowing. This growth outpaces typical inflation and revenue growth.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in absolute debt levels increases refinancing risk and interest rate exposure; lenders track debt-to-revenue ratios to assess repayment capacity under stress.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure peaks at £153.7m in 2027/28—77% higher than the current year outturn
findings.detail: The council's capital program shows a significant spike in 2027/28 at £153.7m, compared to £86.7m in 2025/26 outturn. This frontloading of capital spending will drive borrowing requirements and future revenue pressure.
findings.matters: The scale and timing of capital commitments determine the council's future borrowing needs and revenue obligations; major programs signal either planned investment or deferred spending finally executing.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising steeply—from 12.51% of revenue to 20.32% over five years
findings.detail: The cost of servicing debt is forecast to consume an increasing share of the council's revenue budget, rising 8 percentage points over the forecast period. This trajectory reflects the scale of the planned capital program and likely assumes higher future interest rates than the current position.
findings.matters: A financing cost ratio above 20% of revenue narrows financial headroom and raises lender concerns about debt sustainability and the council's ability to respond to financial shocks.

findings.headline: Workforce capacity is static while council faces increased demands and workloads.
findings.detail: The council identifies workforce capacity reduction as a Key Corporate Risk (KCR9), where reduction may lead to service delivery risk. Compounding this, governance risk detail notes 'increased demands and workloads resulting from any or all of the above with static resources and capacity.' This indicates growing operational pressure with no staffing relief planned.
findings.matters: Static workforce against increasing demands could compromise service delivery quality and the council's financial management capability, potentially affecting its ability to execute strategic initiatives.
findings.figures: No specific staffing figures provided.
findings.quote: Reduction in workforce/ capacity may lead to a risk in service delivery.

findings.headline: May 2027 election delivery is at risk due to boundary commission review with insufficient preparation time.
findings.detail: The Local Government Boundary Commission is reviewing York's electoral arrangements with final outcomes unknown until later in 2026. The council has explicitly flagged that 'insufficient time to make necessary changes will impact on our ability to deliver Local Elections in May 2027 leading to confusion for residents and reputational risk for the Council.' The council is establishing monthly election planning meetings with contingency arrangements.
findings.matters: Election delivery failure represents reputational damage and operational disruption that could undermine public confidence in council governance and financial management.
findings.figures: Election delivery deadline: May 2027.
findings.quote: Insufficient time to make necessary changes will impact on our ability to deliver Local Elections in May 2027 leading to confusion for residents and reputational risk for the Council.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivery is at risk; governance review and resource planning underway.
findings.detail: The council identifies 'failure to deliver the Capital Programme, which includes high profile projects' as a Key Corporate Risk (KCR7). A review of major capital projects governance including resource planning has been completed, and the council is developing a Capital Strategy for 2027/28 with a new Capital Programme assurance process. This remedial action suggests existing delivery concerns.
findings.matters: Capital delivery failures could affect the council's ability to execute planned schemes, and signal project governance weaknesses or resource constraints relevant to lenders.
findings.figures: No specific capital project figures provided.
findings.quote: Failure to deliver the Capital Programme, which includes high profile projects

findings.headline: Government funding cuts continue to reduce council income and impact service delivery.
findings.detail: The council identifies ongoing government funding cuts as a Key Corporate Risk (KCR1) that will continue to impact council services. The S151 Officer has initiated a Fair Funding review consultation response and is developing a Financial Strategy for 2027/28 to address this pressure. This signals the council anticipates sustained income reductions.
findings.matters: Reduced government funding directly constrains the council's financial capacity and affects its ability to meet obligations and service commitments, which is material for lending decisions.
findings.figures: No specific funding reduction figures provided in this monitor.
findings.quote: The Council's increasing collaboration with partnership organisations and ongoing government funding cuts will continue to have an impact on Council services

findings.headline: Investment income declining as interest rates fall
findings.detail: The average rate of return on York's investment portfolio fell from 4.89% in 2024-25 to 4.03% in 2025-26, while the average cash balance available for investment also declined slightly from £29.11m to £27.82m. This reflects both the Bank of England's 75 basis point cuts during the year and the strategy of deploying cash to support capital spending.
findings.matters: Declining investment returns reduce the income available from reserves to support general fund spending or capital investment. This tightens financial flexibility and increases reliance on council tax, fees and charges, or service reductions to balance budgets.
findings.figures: Rate of return 4.03% (2025-26) vs 4.89% (2024-25); average cash balance £27.82m vs £29.11m; SONIA benchmark 4.01% vs 4.90%
findings.quote: The average rate of return achieved for invested cash in the financial year 2025/26 has remained around the average overnight SONIA rate ... compared to 4.89% in the financial year 2024/25

findings.headline: Council maintains under-borrowed position: £163.88m gap between Capital Financing Requirement and actual borrowing
findings.detail: York's CFR is £514.83m but total borrowing is only £350.95m, meaning the council is relying on cash reserves (and investment balances) to cover £163.88m of its capital funding need. This deliberate strategy avoids expensive long-term borrowing but uses up liquid cash reserves that could cover revenue shortfalls.
findings.matters: While the under-borrowed strategy is prudent when borrowing rates are elevated, it creates dependency on cash reserves remaining available. If revenue pressures emerge or capital spending accelerates, the council has less liquidity buffer. The strategy works only if rates fall as forecast.
findings.figures: CFR £514.83m, Total borrowing £350.95m, funding gap £163.88m (30% of CFR); investment balance £4.38m (significantly smaller than funding gap)
findings.quote: the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt, and cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has continued to be used as an interim measure to fund the capital programme

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement came in 10.7% below budget forecast
findings.detail: The actual Capital Financing Requirement for 2025-26 was £514.83m against a forecast of £570.54m in the Treasury Management Strategy Statement approved in February 2025. This £55.71m variance (General Fund £59.46m below, HRA £3.67m below) represents significant underspend or slippage in the capital programme.
findings.matters: Large variance between forecast and outturn suggests either capital programme slippage, underspend against approved investment plans, or re-phasing of expenditure. This affects the council's ability to deliver planned capital schemes and may indicate project delivery issues.
findings.figures: CFR outturn £514.83m vs TMSS forecast £570.54m (variance £55.71m); General Fund £331.95m actual vs £391.41m forecast
findings.quote: CFR General Fund £331.95m [outturn] ... £391.41m [budget forecast]

findings.headline: High concentration of debt maturing in 2026-27 creates refinancing risk
findings.detail: £53.75m of York's £350.95m debt portfolio matures in 2026-27. Of this, £32.80m relates to short-term (1-year or less) loans drawn down in February-March 2026. The council acknowledges this maturity profile will be "higher than originally planned" due to deliberate short-term borrowing decisions taken during the rate spike in March 2026.
findings.matters: The council will face significant refinancing needs next year (15% of total debt). If forecast rate falls do not materialise, refinancing risk is material. The concentration in a single year also limits flexibility if circumstances change.
findings.figures: £53.75m maturing in 2026/27; £32.80m from 1-year or shorter maturity loans drawn March 2026
findings.quote: A total of £53.75m debt will mature in 2026/27, of which £32.80m relates to debt drawn down in 2025/26 with 1 year maturities or less

findings.headline: Temporary local authority borrowing drawn down to manage year-end cash position
findings.detail: In late March 2026, York borrowed £8m for 2.5 months (to 15 June 2026) from another local authority at 4.25%, explicitly to avoid taking on further debt at elevated PWLB rates. This was a tactical short-term measure to cover the end-of-year position when gilt yields had spiked sharply following the Middle East conflict.
findings.matters: Temporary borrowing at higher cost to avoid permanent borrowing signals cash flow pressure at year-end and vulnerability to rate spikes. It suggests the council's capital programme timing or cash reserves created end-of-year strain.
findings.figures: £8.00m temporary loan drawn 30 March 2026, repayable 15 June 2026, at 4.25%
findings.quote: one temporary loan from another Local Authority was drawn down to avoid further borrowing at elevated rates and cover the end of year position

findings.headline: Net external debt growing 39% over five years to £551.7m
findings.detail: Net external debt (gross debt less investments) increases from £396.0m in 2025/26 to £551.7m by 2029/30. Gross debt grows from £400.4m to £556.7m, with cash investments remaining flat at £4.4-5.0m across the period.
findings.matters: Lenders track absolute debt levels and growth trajectory as key risk indicators. A 39% increase in net debt over five years, combined with rising financing costs, signals a council taking on substantial new borrowing obligations.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure programme peaks at £153.7m in 2027/28, 77% above current outturn
findings.detail: Total capital expenditure is projected to peak at £153.7m in 2027/28 (General Fund £113.4m, HRA £39.8m), significantly exceeding the 2025/26 actual outturn of £86.7m, before declining to £58.1m by 2029/30. This concentration reflects concentrated investment spending.
findings.matters: Large capital programmes drive borrowing needs and future debt service costs. A peak programme of £153.7m indicates the council is planning substantial capital investment, with direct implications for the CFR, external debt, and financing costs.

findings.detail: The short-term liquidity requirement component of the operational boundary falls sharply from £65.7m in 2025/26 to £55.7m in 2026/27 and then to £10.0m from 2027/28 onwards. This represents a significant change in the council's cash flow assumptions and liquidity buffer requirements.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand changes in councils' liquidity positions and the drivers behind them. A sharp reduction in required liquidity buffers could indicate either improved cash forecasting or potentially reduced financial resilience.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs to revenue ratio nearly doubles from 12.51% to 20.32% over four years
findings.detail: The proportion of general fund net revenue going to financing costs (including debt service, PFI, and lease payments) increases from 12.51% actual in 2025/26 to 15.98% in 2026/27, 17.94% in 2027/28, 19.69% in 2028/29, and 20.32% in 2029/30. This represents accelerating growth in the debt service burden on council revenue.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors track this ratio closely as a key indicator of debt sustainability. A ratio exceeding 20% means over one-fifth of council revenue is locked into debt service, severely limiting budget flexibility for service spending and indicating unsustainable debt accumulation.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 - Capital Programme Outturn 2025-26 and Revisions to the 2026-27 – 2029-30 Programme - Annex 1
findings.headline: 2027-28 peak year of £153.1m capital expenditure depends significantly on capital receipts (£16.9m) which could deteriorate if property market weakens
findings.detail: The capital programme reaches its peak in 2027-28 at £153.1m. That year requires £16.9m in capital receipts (£10.4m Right to Buy sales, £6.6m property market sales), funding approximately 23% of the year's expenditure. The remaining funding comes from government grants £50.9m and borrowing £68.8m.
findings.matters: Capital receipts from property sales are volatile and externally sensitive. A significant slowdown in the property market or Right to Buy activity in 2027-28 would create a funding gap in the programme's critical peak year, forcing either deferrals or unplanned additional borrowing.

findings.matters: Below-target complaint handling suggests operational backlogs and resource constraints. When combined with the customer service metric (average phone answer time tripling to 2:11), this indicates strains on back-office functions that could affect wider service delivery.

findings.detail: Snapshot count of people sleeping rough increased 136% from 14 to 33. This is marked as a negative direction of travel and indicates acute housing crisis or affordability breakdown affecting the council's most vulnerable residents.
findings.matters: Doubling rough sleeping alongside record housing voids (above) suggests a market mismatch—stock exists but is not being let. This signals affordability or demand-side problems that could constrain the HRA and increase pressure on social services spending.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - 2025-26 Finance and Performance Outturn - Annex 1
findings.headline: Council housing void properties jumped 64% year-on-year, from 81 to 133
findings.detail: Total void properties (excluding non-offerables) increased from 81 to 133, with standard voids rising from 55 to 118 and major works voids from 7 to 15. This represents a significant deterioration in asset utilisation within the housing revenue account.
findings.matters: Void properties represent lost rental income on a council-owned asset. A 52-unit increase in vacancies directly reduces the HRA's rental income base and suggests either asset management issues or reduced housing demand in the area.

findings.headline: ASC mitigation projects forecast £1.312k savings but delivered £1.597k, with some initiatives yielding no savings
findings.detail: ASC had approved savings of £1.140k plus £358k from business efficiencies. In-year, it revised its mitigation plans to £1.312k expected savings. Outturn shows £1.597k delivered (overachievement), but this masks uneven delivery: Section 117 funding recovered only £480k of £974k forecast; some projects (ASC05 Transport, ASC06) delivered £0 savings in-year; Direct Payment audits overachieved at £552k against £142k forecast. The service is 'continually reviewing opportunities' but savings delivery is volatile.
findings.matters: Savings plans are how the council plans to balance future budgets. If mitigation projects are unreliable (some hitting zero, some overachieving), the council's medium-term financial plan is at risk.
findings.figures: Approved savings £1.140k; business efficiencies £358k; mitigation total £1.312k; actual delivery £1.597k; Section 117 £480k of £974k; DP audits £552k of £142k
findings.quote: Some of the mitigation project overachieved the forecasted savings, however some did not yield any savings within the year.

findings.headline: Supported Living voids of £425k highlight provider payment model risk and capacity underutilisation
findings.detail: Supported Living schemes that are not at full capacity still require the council to pay providers for empty beds (voids). This generated a £425k overspend to budget. The council notes this 'is a priority area of ASC with a project in place to ensure all schemes are utilised to their full capacity.' A business case is underway to investigate longer-term needs and whether building new provision is required.
findings.matters: Void payments suggest the council has committed to capacity it is not using, likely due to either over-procurement of places or inability to discharge service users into them. This is a structural cost until resolved.
findings.figures: Supported Living voids £425k overspend to budget
findings.quote: Where Supported Living schemes/ settings are not at full capacity, payments are made by CYC to providers for VOIDs. The VOIDs were overspent by £425k to budget.

findings.headline: Capital programme significantly underspent, with borrowing £58m below plan, masking true financing need
findings.detail: The Treasury budget was based on needing £78m of new loans for capital spend. In reality, the council only took out £20m (excluding replacement finance). The council states it has 'a policy of delaying borrowing for as long as possible.' This reduced interest costs by £3.4m in-year, but it means capital slippage is severe and the true financing position may be worse than headline figures suggest.
findings.matters: Delayed borrowing is not free; it defers rather than eliminates costs. Large capital underspends suggest either projects slipping or the capital programme being unaffordable, both of which are concerning for a lender.
findings.figures: Budgeted borrowing £78m; actual borrowing £20m; treasury underspend £3.424m
findings.quote: The underspend on borrowing costs is largely due to lower spending on the capital programme than was budgeted for. The original budget was based on needing an additional £78m of loans to cover the projected capital spend; in the event we only took out £20m of new loans (excluding replacement finance).

findings.headline: Council housing void rate doubled in one year: 55 to 118 properties
findings.detail: Council housing void properties increased from 55 at end of March 2025 to 118 at end of March 2026. The paper attributes this to 'workforce capacity constraints, limited availability of contractors for capital and major void works' and 'new-build and refurbished homes creating additional secondary voids as existing tenants downsize.' This directly reduces rental income and suggests either capital programme slippage or operational capacity issues.
findings.matters: Voids are lost rental income and indicate either capital investment is creating transition voids or the council cannot process repairs fast enough. At typical rates, this could represent ~£200k+ annual rental income loss.
findings.figures: Voids 31 March 2025: 55; voids 31 March 2026: 118; increase of 63 properties (115%)

findings.headline: Building Control service collapsed due to staffing shortages, generating £384k income shortfall
findings.detail: Planning Services had a staff shortage in Building Control 'which has resulted in a minimal chargeable service being in operation.' This generated a £384k income shortfall against budget in one year. The council states 'a recovery plan is underway to ensure a stable service is in place for next year.' General planning application income also shortfalled by £130k. This represents a loss of controllable income, not a cut to a grant.
findings.matters: Chargeable services like Building Control are revenue sources that must be maintained. A £384k loss shows the council cannot always fill staffing gaps, and recovery depends on hiring and retaining staff.
findings.figures: Building Control income shortfall £384k; general planning applications shortfall £130k
findings.quote: within Planning Services there has been a shortage of staff across Building Control during the year which has resulted in a minimal chargeable service being in operation. As a result, the shortfall in income was £384k.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care package costs and numbers growing, outpacing budget allocations across all service types
findings.detail: Nearly every ASC service line shows both increased package numbers AND increased average weekly costs: Direct Payments average cost up £193/week (LD) and £145/week (P&SI/OP); Supported Living weekly costs up £561/week despite reduced package numbers; Residential Older People packages increased 20% above budget with 15% cost increase; Nursing placements up 8 above budget with 15% cost increase; Short-term placements saw a 93% overspend driven by emergency and respite demand. This suggests both demographic/needs-driven growth and inflation outpacing budget provisions.
findings.matters: This isn't a one-year blip but a pattern of recurring cost growth that the council cannot control through volume management alone. If packages are both increasing in number AND cost, the council faces a structural budget problem.
findings.figures: Direct Payments £1.218m overspend (20.5%); Supported Living £2.890m (15.6%); Residential £2.387m (11.7%); Nursing £1.100m (18.2%); cost per week increases: LD DP £193, P&SI £145, SL £561, Residential OP 15%, Nursing 15%
findings.quote: The outturn overspend for Nursing care placements is due to increases in OP and PSI in both the package numbers and weekly rate compared to budget

findings.headline: Council faces 'extremely challenging' financial outlook with government grants declining while pressures grow
findings.detail: The council explicitly states 'the financial outlook for the council over the coming few years is extremely challenging with government grants reducing at the same rate that council tax is increasing.' ASC alone received £10.3m growth in the 2026-27 budget but still will require 'significant savings and mitigation plans' to bring the budget position back in line given the £9m outturn overspend. The council notes that 'most councils have increased council tax at the maximum level allowable' and references 'significant' numbers of councils receiving Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.matters: This is the council's own assessment that it is in a structurally difficult position. It cannot grow its way out (grants declining, tax base capped), and existing services are growing faster than budget (ASC). Lenders need to know whether the council's medium-term financial plan is credible.
findings.figures: ASC growth 2026-27: £10.3m; ASC outturn overspend 2025-26: £9m; government grants described as reducing
findings.quote: the financial outlook for the council over the coming few years is extremely challenging with government grants reducing at the same rate that council tax is increasing

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account working balance falling sharply from debt repayments: £25.8m to £18.0m in one year
findings.detail: The HRA has now made three Self-Financing debt repayments totalling £19.8m (£1.9m in 2024, £8.4m in 2025, £9.5m in 2026). These are funded from HRA reserves. The working balance dropped from £25.8m to £18.0m in one year. The total self-financing debt outstanding is £121.5m (contracted in 2012). At this rate of repayment, reserves will be severely constrained.
findings.matters: HRA debt repayments lock capital into debt service, reducing flexibility for housing investment or responding to pressures. If reserves are depleted, the council loses its financial buffer for the housing service.
findings.figures: Working balance 31 March 2025: £25.8m; working balance 31 March 2026: £18.0m; repayments made £1.9m, £8.4m, £9.5m; total debt £121.5m
findings.quote: The levels of working balance has allowed for the initial repayments £121.5m debt that the HRA incurred as part of self-financing in 2012. The first repayment of £1.9m was paid in March 2024 and a second payment on £8.4m was repaid in March 2025 and a further payment of £9.5m was repaid in March 2026.

findings.headline: General reserves only cover the ASC overspend once; council adding underspend to reserves as buffer
findings.detail: General reserves currently stand at £7.4m minimum requirement. The council is adding the full £1.498m underspend to reserves, bringing them to £8.898m. However, this is barely 5.7% of net budget, and the ASC overspend alone (£9m) now exceeds total reserves. The position has only improved this year because of one-off items: £2.3m windfall business rates income from Leeds City Region pool and £3.4m underspend on Treasury costs from lower-than-planned borrowing.
findings.matters: Reserves are the buffer against unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. If the ASC overspend recurs and one-off items don't materialise, the council would need to use reserves or cut spending.
findings.figures: General reserves £7.4m minimum; will be £8.898m after adding underspend; net budget £156.921m; ASC overspend £8.996m; one-off business rates £2.3m; one-off treasury saving £3.4m
findings.quote: the result of the underspend there has been no need to draw on general reserves which stand at £7.4m

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant moving into persistent deficit as Safety Valve funding ends after 2025-26
findings.detail: The DSG brought forward balance was £592k surplus at 1 April 2025, but after an in-year deficit of £1.256m ended at £664k deficit at 31 March 2026. Critically, this position included £2m of Safety Valve recovery funding (now ended). Without that support, the in-year deficit would have been £3.256m. Going forward, 'the DSG will be under significant financial pressures.' The council also notes 'it is becoming increasingly difficult for High Needs pupils to be supported in mainstream school settings' due to low school funding.
findings.matters: The DSG is a ring-fenced account; deficits accrue and must be recovered. This shows the council is hitting the third year of a four-year Safety Valve recovery plan but the underlying deficit position is unsustainable without external funding.
findings.figures: £592k brought forward surplus; £1.256m in-year deficit; £2m Safety Valve funding (final year); final position £664k deficit; hypothetical deficit without Safety Valve £3.256m
findings.quote: 2025/26 was the final year of Safety Valve funding and the council received £2m funding this year. Going forward into future years the DSG will be under significant financial pressures.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £8.996m is deteriorating and putting pressure on the council's overall financial position
findings.detail: ASC outturn worsened by £1.75m from the Monitor 3 forecast (£7.246m to £8.996m). The service is 15.4% over budget. Direct Payments overspend by £1.218m, Supported Living by £2.890m (with £425k from unfilled capacity), and Residential Care by £2.387m driven by increased package numbers and higher average weekly costs. The council describes this as 'concerning' and states it took 'significant work across other service areas' to bring year end to a small surplus.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can sustain this level of recurring overspend. At £9m, it's 5.7% of the entire net budget and would wipe out a significant portion of general reserves if it happens again.
findings.figures: £8.996m overspend (15.4% of £58.533m budget); worsened by £1.750m since Monitor 3; £7.25m predicted at Monitor 3
findings.quote: The key area that requires continued council wide focus is Adult Social Care where the overspend of £8,996k is putting pressure on the council's overall position.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 - Capital Programme Outturn 2025-26 and Revisions to the 2026-27 – 2029-30 Programme
findings.headline: Bell Farm refurbishment exceeded budget due to unforeseen site conditions including asbestos and bats
findings.detail: The 40-apartment Bell Farm refurbishment project overran and exceeded budget after encountering asbestos, bats, drainage replacement issues, and delayed water connections. This suggests inadequate pre-project surveys or site investigation, with costs now being absorbed.

findings.paper_title: Annex B City of York Council - Auditor's Annual Report 24-25 FINAL DRAFT (ID 2534697)
findings.headline: Cash reserves fell to £1.8m requiring new short-term PWLB borrowing with refinancing risk in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council's cash position deteriorated significantly in 2023/24 to £1.8m due to internal borrowing for capital expenditure and cost pressures, down from £13.2m in prior year. This heightened liquidity risk. The council borrowed six times from PWLB in short-term durations during 2024/25, each loan maturing in 2025/26 and requiring refinancing. The use of short maturity durations increases refinancing interest rate risk, though within prudential limits. Cash recovered to £8.9m by March 2025.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about the council's liquidity vulnerability and exposure to refinancing risk. Short-term borrowing concentrated in a single year means borrowing costs are sensitive to PWLB rate changes and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Cash balance £1.8m (31 March 2024), £8.9m (31 March 2025); six new short-term PWLB loans require refinancing in 2025/26
findings.quote: As a result of this, and the elevated Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) rates, the Council part funded the capital programme by internal borrowing and used their cash balances where available. This resulted in a significantly lower cash balance of £1.8m as at 31 March 2024 in comparison to £13.2m in the year prior. The Council's liquidity risk was therefore heightened in the short-term. As a result, new borrowing was required in the first and last quarter of 2024/25. The Council has taken six new short-term loans from the PWLB which will require refinancing in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Capital schemes that do not complete will have costs charged to revenue
findings.detail: The council rates medium likelihood and high seriousness that 'Capital costs may have to be charged to revenue, should a scheme not progress to completion.' This is a mechanism for capital slippage to damage revenue budgets.
findings.matters: Schemes that slip force emergency revenue funding, which either requires spending cuts to services or deepens revenue budget pressure
findings.figures: medium likelihood / high seriousness
findings.quote: Capital costs may have to be charged to revenue, should a scheme not progress to completion.

findings.headline: Capital programme expansion is expected to increase borrowing costs
findings.detail: The council flags medium likelihood and high seriousness that its capital programme expansion will 'increase in the capital programme' leading to higher borrowing costs, plus separate medium-likelihood medium-seriousness risk of 'Short or medium term cashflow impact' from the same expansion. This is particularly acute in a rising interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Higher borrowing costs reduce resources available for service delivery; cashflow pressure can constrain the council's operational liquidity
findings.figures: medium likelihood / high seriousness on borrowing costs
findings.quote: Increased costs of borrowing due to increase in the capital programme

findings.headline: General reserves are at risk of falling below minimum levels
findings.detail: The council identifies medium-high likelihood and high seriousness that it could fall below its minimum reserve threshold if budgets exceed targets. Reserves falling below minimum is a governance and credit-worthiness concern—it signals loss of financial control.
findings.matters: Minimum reserves exist as a buffer against shocks; falling below them signals financial distress to lenders and regulators and removes that protection
findings.figures: medium-high likelihood / high seriousness
findings.quote: Potential for reserves to go below minimum levels due to budgets being exceeded

findings.headline: Mitigations (cost-control measures) outlined in monitoring reports may fail to land
findings.detail: The council rates medium-high likelihood and high seriousness that 'mitigations not being delivered as outlined in monitoring reports'. Budget mitigations are the assumptions on which the financial strategy is built—if they don't land in year, there is no pre-planned solution.
findings.matters: Undelivered mitigations create unbudgeted overspend mid-year with no alternative funding source already identified
findings.figures: medium-high likelihood / high seriousness
findings.quote: Budgets across the Council are overspent due to mitigations not being delivered as outlined in monitoring reports

findings.headline: Adult social care faces both demand pressures and Better Care Fund underperformance risks
findings.detail: The council identifies two separate high-seriousness risks in adult care: external demand creating 'increased clients in adult care' (medium-high likelihood, high seriousness) and 'Underperformance of Better Care Fund schemes' (high likelihood, high seriousness). Adult social care is the largest and least controllable council budget nationally.
findings.matters: Runaway adult care costs directly threaten the council's financial stability and debt service capacity, and they are very difficult to reverse mid-year
findings.figures: two risks rated high seriousness; BCF risk is high likelihood
findings.quote: Budgets across the Council are overspent due to external pressures eg increased clients in adult care

findings.headline: Savings plans are at high risk of non-delivery due to reduced management capacity
findings.detail: The council rates as high likelihood and high seriousness that its planned savings 'will not be achieved, or delayed' specifically because of 'reduced management and support services capacity to deliver'. This is the most serious risk in the register because planned savings are built into the financial strategy as essential to balance the budget—if capacity cannot deliver them, the entire strategy fails.
findings.matters: Savings plans are the foundation of council financial stability; if management lacks capacity to deliver them, unplanned overspend follows with no funding solution
findings.figures: high likelihood / high seriousness
findings.quote: All Savings are not achieved, or delayed, due to reduced management and support services capacity to deliver

findings.paper_title: Item 9 - Treasury Management 2025-26 Quarter 3 report and review of Prudential Indicators - Annex A
findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising from 13.8% to 20.1% of net revenue over the medium term
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream for the General Fund increases steadily from 13.80% in 2025/26 to 20.09% by 2029/30 — a 45% increase over five years. By contrast, HRA financing costs remain stable (12.31% declining to 10.91%), indicating the pressure is concentrated on the general fund side. This means debt servicing will consume an increasing share of the council's revenue budget.
findings.matters: A rising financing cost ratio reduces financial flexibility and resilience. A council spending one-fifth of revenue on debt servicing has limited capacity to respond to demand pressures, absorb grant reductions, or fund service changes. Lenders view this as a key indicator of credit deterioration.

findings.headline: York Outer Ring Road - Dualling concentrates £28.45m (67%) of its four-year spend in 2029-30
findings.detail: The ring road scheme totals £42,601k but shows highly skewed timing: £2,150k (2026-27), £6,000k (2027-28), £6,000k (2028-29), then £28,451k (2029-30). This back-loading creates a major peak in capital requirement and borrowing need in the final year.
findings.matters: Lumpy spending profiles concentrate liquidity and borrowing needs into single years. Understanding project timing is essential for assessing debt management capacity and cash flow constraints in specific years.
findings.figures: York Outer Ring Road - Dualling: £2,150k, £6,000k, £6,000k, £28,451k across four years
findings.quote: York Outer Ring Road - Dualling 2,150 6,000 6,000 28,451 42,601

findings.headline: The capital programme has contingency of £500k in 2026-27 but zero contingency in years 2-4
findings.detail: The capital contingency fund shows £500k in year one, then £0 in each of the following three years. For a £383m multi-year programme, there is no explicit reserve to absorb cost overruns, project acceleration, or scope changes in three-quarters of the programme period.
findings.matters: Absence of contingency limits financial flexibility—any cost variance or project change in years 2-4 would require either reallocation from other schemes or additional borrowing. This affects both project delivery risk and debt levels.
findings.quote: Capital Contingency 500 0 0 0 500

findings.headline: Corporate prudential borrowing of £120m is the single largest internal funding source for the capital programme
findings.detail: The council plans to use £120,022k in corporate prudential borrowing across the four years, distributed as £42,961k (2026-27), £28,011k (2027-28), £24,649k (2028-29), and £24,401k (2029-30). This represents 31% of total capital expenditure and is the dominant internal funding source, substantially ahead of all other funding mechanisms.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the magnitude and profile of new borrowing planned and its impact on total debt service obligations. A commitment to borrow £120m over four years is material to debt sustainability analysis.
findings.figures: Corporate Prudential Borrowing: £120,022k total; annual amounts £42,961k, £28,011k, £24,649k, £24,401k
findings.quote: Corporate Prudential Borrowing 42,961 28,011 24,649 24,401 120,022

findings.headline: Energy Retrofit Wave 3 programme delayed by recruitment difficulties on £1.4m three-year grant
findings.detail: The council has secured £1.4m in grant funding over three years from April 2025 to improve energy efficiency in council social housing. However, difficulties in recruiting the right staff have delayed the start of this project. No specific timeline for project start is given.
findings.matters: A three-year energy efficiency programme is not yet executing due to staffing constraints, putting grant funding draw-down at risk and delaying carbon reduction commitments on council housing.
findings.figures: £1.4m grant funding over 3 years (April 2025 onwards).
findings.quote: A new scheme (wave 3) is for 3 years, recently signed, will provide £1.4m of grant funding over 3 years to continue to improve the energy efficiency across the CYC social housing stock. Difficulties in recruitment of the right staff are meaning that there are delays to the start of this project.

findings.headline: EV charging contractor has failed to honour contract terms and installation works are delayed to 2026/27
findings.detail: Under the EVCAR scheme, the contracted EV supply and install operator can no longer honour the terms of their contract. The council has received a refund of payments for charger installation works at Bishopthorpe Road and Monk Bar Car Park locations. These works will now be rescheduled to 2026/27 pending procurement of a new EV supply/install/maintenance contract.
findings.matters: A contracted supplier has failed to deliver and the council must re-procure, delaying infrastructure investment and requiring new contractor engagement during an energy transition initiative.
findings.figures: Charger installations delayed from 2025/26 to 2026/27.
findings.quote: EVCAR has received a refund from the contracted EV supply and install operator who can no longer honour the terms of their contract. Payments relating to charger installation works at Bishopthorpe Road and Monk Bar Car Park locations have been returned and works will now take place during 26/27 once a new EV supply/install/maintenance contract has been awarded.

findings.headline: Capital budget cut by £23.4m at Monitor 3 (13% of approved budget) indicating weak original forecasting
findings.detail: The capital programme was approved in February 2025 at £180.743m. After a £0.412m adjustment at Monitor 1, the council is now reporting a £23.432m reduction at Monitor 3, leaving £139.034m. This mid-year cut of 13% suggests the original February forecast significantly overestimated delivery or affordability across departments.
findings.matters: Nearly one-seventh of the approved capital budget is being removed at Q3, indicating poor original planning and forecasting. For a lender, this raises questions about the reliability of financial planning and departmental delivery expectations.
findings.figures: Approved 2025/26 budget £180.743m, Monitor 1 adjustment £0.412m, Monitor 3 decrease £23.432m, revised budget £139.034m. Reduction represents 12.9% of original approved budget.
findings.quote: At Monitor 1 report (September 2nd, 2025) there was a decrease of £0.412m resulting in a revised capital programme of £180.331m. A decrease of £23.432m is detailed in this monitor resulting in a revised capital programme for 2025/26 of £139.034m.

findings.headline: Mansion House contractor has issued formal delay notice on rear elevation works due to structural complications
findings.detail: Contractor W Birch has issued a contractual notice of delay warning that the completion date may be missed, specifically relating to rear elevation raking out and repointing work which has proven more extensive than expected. Dangerous brickwork has been identified requiring removal and structural supports being inserted. The council has taken partial possession with no public access to affected areas while remedial work is resolved.
findings.matters: A listed building conservation project has received a formal contractor delay notice, indicating the works are progressing to schedule pressure. The council is incurring additional structural work not originally budgeted and is managing partial facility closure.
findings.figures: Notice of delay issued. Completion previously expected 5 December 2025, now extended. Final completion expected end of January 2026.
findings.quote: Notice of delay has been received from W Birch, this is currently a contractual mechanism to warn the client completion date could be missed and this is in relation to the rear elevation works. However, no extension of time is anticipated at this stage which could incur additional costs.

findings.headline: Transport capital programme re-profiled by £12m (21% of budget) due to review of project commitments
findings.detail: The Transport, Highways and Environment directorate's budget is being reduced by £12.015m of the £58.062m total, all through re-profiling to future years. The paper states this is 'mainly due to a review of Transport project commitments' but does not specify which projects or what commitments changed. This represents a substantial reassessment of transport delivery plans.
findings.matters: Over one-fifth of the transport capital budget has been pushed into future years due to a mid-year review of project commitments, suggesting delivery or affordability issues across multiple transport schemes that were not apparent when the budget was set in February.
findings.figures: £12.015m re-profiled from £58.062m budget (21% of directorate budget).
findings.quote: A decrease of £23.432m is detailed in this monitor resulting in a revised capital programme for 2025/26 of £139.034m. There is an increase of £1.4m due to additional funding being awarded / approved and a re-profiling of budgets to future years totalling £24.834m. This is mainly due to a review of Transport project commitments.

findings.headline: York Outer Ring Road costs have escalated sharply enough to require four-phase delivery instead of planned approach
findings.detail: After initial planning approval in April 2024, the council undertook a milestone review in July 2025 which identified increased anticipated costs. Members agreed to restructure from the original delivery plan into four phases to prioritise available funding against local plan infrastructure and new homes requirements. This represents a material cost escalation requiring project restructuring.
findings.matters: A major strategic infrastructure scheme's costs have escalated mid-project to the point where the delivery model had to be restructured and phased. This indicates cost forecasting issues at project approval stage.
findings.figures: Project restructured from planned approach to four phases due to 'increased anticipated costs'.
findings.quote: Members agreed at Meeting on 15th July as a result of the milestone review that the scheme be delivered in four phases, due to the increased anticipated costs. This prioritises available funding to the local plan infrastructure requirements, unlocking key development sites and providing much needed new homes.

findings.headline: York Station Gateway now 18 months late with unforeseen ground conditions and listed building complications
findings.detail: This major transport infrastructure project's Package 2 (Highways Works) was originally due to complete in September 2024 but now has a projected completion date of Spring 2026. Unforeseen ground conditions have been encountered and the Portico Canopy requires Listed Building Consent for demolition. The multi-package structure has created delivery interdependencies between CYC, LNER, Network Rail and partners.
findings.matters: A major council-led infrastructure package is significantly delayed with cost and scheduling implications. The project's multi-party structure and discovery of unforeseen conditions mid-build indicates prior surveying gaps.
findings.figures: Original completion September 2024, current projection Spring 2026 (18+ month delay).
findings.quote: The works are currently delayed against the original programme with the projected completion date being Spring 2026, (original completion date September 2024). Site works continue in Zone 12 the Portico Area & Tea Room Square, unforeseen ground conditions have been experienced and the Portico Canopy located in the area is now subject to a Listed Building Consent to allow for demolition.

findings.headline: Bell Farm refurbishment now 44% over budget with £2.1m additional cost
findings.detail: The Bell Farm refurbishment originally budgeted at £4.831m across 3 years is now forecast to cost £6.940m total. Unforeseen site conditions including asbestos, bats, building defects, drainage issues, and delayed water connections have driven cumulative overspends from £1.2m at outturn (2024/25) to £1.368m at Monitor 1, now to £2.109m total. Project completion has slipped and is now set for end of March 2026.
findings.matters: A major housing refurbishment is significantly over budget and late, with cost escalation now 44% above original approved budget. Additional costs are being absorbed from Major Repairs underspend, putting pressure on that already-strained programme.
findings.figures: Original budget £4.831m, forecast £6.940m, overspend £2.109m (44%). 2024/25 outturn overspend £1.2m, Monitor 1 £1.368m, Monitor 3 £2.109m.
findings.quote: The scheme had a budget of £4.831m, profiled across 3 years. The 2024/25 outturn reported an overspend of £1.2m. At Monitor 1, this had increased to £1.368m. The latest forecast is a total spend of £6.940m which is a total overspend of £2.109m. The increase in spend is largely due to the ongoing delays of the works resulting in uplifts to the contractor payments.

findings.headline: Major Repairs programme vacancy and underspend driven by staffing crisis
findings.detail: The Investment Manager post in Housing Major Repairs has been vacant since April 2025 with continued staff absences throughout the year. A temporary 3-month manager was appointed while permanent recruitment proceeded. This reduced capacity has resulted in an anticipated underspend from £11.774m budget to £10.3m forecast spend, with only £6m delivered to date.
findings.matters: A core housing maintenance programme is under-running due to lack of permanent leadership and team capacity, which delays adaptations, empty property repairs, and damp works on council housing stock.
findings.figures: £11.774m budgeted, £10.3m forecast (£1.474m underspend). £6m spent to date.
findings.quote: The Investment Manager post became vacant in April 2025 and there have been continued staff absences within the team for most of the year. A temporary manager was appointed for 3 months while a permanent appointment could be made. This has resulted in reduced capacity across the service and has resulted in an anticipated underspend across these budget areas.

findings.headline: The four-year capital programme growth of £42.18m is 90% externally funded, limiting new council debt.
findings.detail: Of £42.18m total capital growth planned for 2026-27 to 2029-30, external funding from Combined Authority and Government grants totals £37.95m, comprising highway maintenance (£6m), Local Transport Fund (£24.05m), and bus service infrastructure (£7.9m). The council's own contribution is just £1.91m from prudential borrowing and £2.32m from HRA funding.
findings.matters: Dependence on external grant funding means the programme could be disrupted by changes in grant availability, but it demonstrates the council is appropriately minimising new debt-funded capital investment.
findings.figures: Total growth £42,180k; external funding £37,950k; council borrowing £1,910k; HRA funding £2,320k

findings.headline: York is approving £1.91m in prudential borrowing for capital growth, all concentrated in 2026-27.
findings.detail: The council is borrowing to fund new schemes including crematorium refurbishment (£585k), fire resilience building improvements (£200k), fleet replacement (£625k), and a £500k contingency. This borrowing generates a revenue cost of £179k in 2027-28. No further council borrowing for capital is planned in subsequent years of the four-year programme.
findings.matters: For a lender, new borrowing and the revenue costs it commits to are central to assessing financial sustainability. The concentration of borrowing in one year followed by no further borrowing in the planning period suggests a managed capital investment approach.
findings.figures: £1,910k prudential borrowing in 26/27; £179k revenue cost in 27/28
findings.quote: Total CYC Prudential Borrowing 1,910      -          -          -     1,910

findings.headline: Council housing rents rising 4.5% to £39.6m as primary HRA funding source
findings.detail: Rental income from council housing is increasing from £37.9m to £39.6m (+£1.7m), driving income growth at 4.5%. This is the HRA's largest income stream and is fuelling growth in both debt servicing capacity and reserve contributions.
findings.matters: The HRA's financial plan depends entirely on sustained rent increases; if rent policy tightens—due to affordability pressures, welfare changes, or political constraints—the reserve contributions will become unaffordable and deficits will widen
findings.figures: Council housing rent income: £37.9m (2025/26) to £39.6m (2026/27); increase £1.7m or 4.5%
