findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account carries forward cumulative deficit of £10.5m into 2026-27
findings.detail: The HRA opened 2025/26 with a carried-forward deficit of £25.8m. After deficits of £7.5m and £7.8m in consecutive years, this has improved to £10.5m—but a material negative balance persists. The cumulative deficit represents unresolved past financial pressures in the housing service.
findings.matters: A decade-scale carried-forward deficit suggests either past underinvestment, rents held below cost, or capital pressures that have accumulated; its persistence into 2026-27 indicates ongoing structural issues
findings.figures: Deficit brought forward 2025/26: £25.8m; deficit carried forward 2026/27: £10.5m
findings.quote: -25,816 (SURPLUS) / DEFICIT BROUGHT FORWARD -18,339 ... -18,339 (SURPLUS) / DEFICIT CARRIED FORWARD -10,494

findings.headline: HRA records £7.8m deficit in 2026-27 after £10.6m contribution to earmarked reserves despite operational surplus
findings.detail: The HRA generates an operational surplus of £7.7m (income exceeds day-to-day expenditure), but after debt servicing (£5.2m interest paid), capital from revenue (£840k), and a substantial contribution to earmarked reserves (£10.6m), records a year-on-year deficit of £7.8m. This pattern shows the council is deliberately building HRA reserves despite being unable to fully self-finance.
findings.matters: Large, sustained reserve contributions while running deficits suggests the council anticipates significant future housing pressures—capital needs, welfare changes, or affordability constraints—that make it feel compelled to build a buffer
findings.figures: Net cost of service surplus £7.7m; contribution to earmarked reserves £10.6m; deficit in year £7.8m
findings.quote: 9,500 Contribution to/(from) Earmarked Reserves 10,600 ... 7,477 (SURPLUS) / DEFICIT IN YEAR 7,845

findings.headline: Budget depends on £4,500k saving from reduction in employer superannuation rates
findings.detail: The council is planning to save £4,500k by benefiting from a reduction in employer superannuation contribution rates. This is 41% of total planned savings of £10,918k. If the rate reduction does not occur or is reversed, the council would face a £4,500k shortfall.
findings.matters: This saving is contingent on external rate changes beyond the council's control; lenders assess budget risk and need to understand whether savings plans depend on assumptions that could reverse.
findings.figures: £4,500k superannuation saving (41% of £10,918k total savings)
findings.quote: Saving arising from reduction in employer superannuation rate (4,500)

findings.headline: Adult services facing £10,330k in demographic and price pressures
findings.detail: Adult services costs are rising by £10,330k due to demographic changes and price inflation combined. This is the single largest cost pressure in the budget and reflects structural demand from an aging population unlikely to reverse.
findings.matters: This structural, recurring demand pressure shows the council faces ongoing cost growth in a key service area; lenders need to understand whether funding can be sustained for these commitments.
findings.figures: £10,330k adult services prices and demographic pressure
findings.quote: Adults Services: Prices and Demographic 10,330

findings.headline: Revenue cost of borrowing increasing by £2,328k
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget includes an additional £2,328k in revenue cost of borrowing, reflecting either higher levels of borrowing or rising interest rates. This represents new debt servicing pressure within a tightly balanced budget.
findings.matters: Lenders need to track whether councils can sustain debt servicing costs; rising borrowing costs reduce financial flexibility and indicate either increasing leverage or exposure to interest rate risk.
findings.figures: £2,328k revenue cost of borrowing
findings.quote: Revenue cost of borrowing 2,328

findings.headline: York proposes funding transformation programme costs with £2.5m of capital receipts to deliver £4.3m of savings
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £4.3m of proposed savings, many to be delivered through a transformation programme. The council plans to finance transformation costs and technology investment from capital receipts under government flexibility rules, with £750k specifically earmarked for transformation revenue costs.
findings.matters: This shows the council is using finite capital resources to fund transformation that must deliver recurring savings; if transformation underperforms, capital receipts are spent without achieving the savings.
findings.figures: £4.3m savings proposed, £2.5m capital receipts proposed for qualifying expenditure, £750k earmarked for transformation revenue costs
findings.quote: The proposals set out in the 2026/27 budget include a further £4.3m of savings many of which will be identified through working differently. The Council's transformation programme is intended to deliver these savings, and it is therefore proposed that the costs of delivering the transformation programme are funded from a proportion of the capital receipts the council holds and intends to obtain during the financial year.

findings.headline: Business support savings of £200k depend on successful AI tool implementation for meeting note automation—an unproven technology.
findings.detail: HRS01 proposes £67k (2026-27) and £133k (2027-28) from 'automated note making in meetings resulting in reduced need for business support resource.' This assumes AI tools work as promised and staff costs are variable or redeployed. AI-dependent staffing reductions are unproven; if tools underperform or staff prove sticky, the savings won't land.
findings.matters: Staffing reductions dependent on unproven technology are high-risk. If tools fail to deliver as assumed, the council will need alternative savings or face budget gaps.
findings.quote: Savings arising from automated note making in meetings resulting in reduced need for business support resource.

findings.headline: Homelessness service savings of £200k follow recent insourcing and depend on restructuring efficiency and sustained external funding.
findings.detail: HCS02 proposes £200k savings after the council insourced homelessness services. Savings depend on 'maximising external funding' and reducing B&B accommodation. Insourcing is recent, and immediately pursuing efficiency savings suggests the council is still learning true costs. If external funders withdraw or B&B demand doesn't fall as assumed, the council loses this £200k (with no year-two recurrence).
findings.matters: Homelessness cost volatility directly affects council finances. Lenders track whether councils have sustainable funding models for demand-led services.
findings.quote: Following the insourcing of services, review of structures to improve efficiency, maximising external funding and reducing levels of B&B accommodation and associated costs to the council.

findings.headline: Income-generating savings of £250k depend on external behaviour: holiday let waste take-up, garden waste subscriptions, developer engagement.
findings.detail: ERS02 forecasts £100-150k from waste services to holiday lets. ERS03 expects £100k from full-year garden waste collection (zero recurrence). ERS05 expects £50k from developer planning performance agreements. These depend on external uptake and sustained engagement, which is less controllable than cost reduction and typically more volatile.
findings.matters: Income-dependent savings often slip or prove volatile. A lender tracking cash flow stability needs to know if these proposals are at risk.
findings.quote: Additional income from providing services to holiday lets

findings.headline: Children's services savings of £1.2m depend on successful transition to in-house provision, explicitly to reverse over-reliance on expensive external markets.
findings.detail: CES02 (£340k) creates in-house supported accommodation for unaccompanied young people. CES03 continues placement cost reduction (£500k). The council explicitly states this to reduce 'over reliance on an expensive external placement market.' If in-house delivery costs more than forecast or slips, these savings will not land. Zero year-two impact suggests no recurring benefit or no confidence in sustainability.
findings.matters: The council is betting £1.2m of its budget on complex service model changes. A lender tracking operational risk needs to know if these transitions succeed and whether placement costs stay within forecast.
findings.quote: Reduced placement costs as a result of developing in house supported accommodation for Unaccompanied Young People, this has reduced our over reliance on an expensive external placement market.

findings.headline: First-year savings of £4.3m drop by 58% to £1.8m in year two, suggesting most proposals are one-off or face sustainability risk.
findings.detail: The council's savings plan shows £4.3m in 2026-27 but only £1.8m in 2027-28. Scanning the proposals, most show zero impact in year two. This cliff suggests either one-time savings, successful implementation that doesn't repeat, or delivery risk the council is not flagging. If budget pressure continues, the council will need new savings to offset the drop.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's budget stability needs to know whether these savings hold the budget, or whether the council is dependent on annual savings initiatives that may slip.
findings.quote: TOTAL SAVINGS 4,293 1,816 6,109

findings.headline: High Needs Block (SEND) facing £1.8m deficit after safety valve ends
findings.detail: The High Needs Block DSG is frozen at 2025/26 levels with only 0.1% increase, despite rising SEND demand. The council's safety valve agreement (providing £2m additional grant) ends 31 March 2026 with no new agreements to follow. Prior to the white paper, the council forecasts high needs expenditure will exceed the DSG grant allocation by £1.8m in 2026/27, resulting in cumulative DSG deficit of £0.6m by March 2027, with continuing and increasing deficits forecast in future years. Statutory override for SEND DSG deficits ends after 2027/28 and conditions for accessing support remain unannounced.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit signals inability to fund statutory SEND provision within available resources. The end of statutory override means the council will face accountability for accumulated deficits with uncertain support from government, affecting financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 2025/26 high needs allocation: £32.139m; 2026/27 allocation: £32.179m (0.1% increase); Forecast in-year deficit 2026/27: £1.8m; Cumulative DSG deficit by 31 March 2027: £0.6m; Safety valve funding: £2m (ending 31 March 2026)
findings.quote: The combined impact of the ending of the safety valve contribution and the freezing of the high needs allocation at the 2025/26 level creates a challenging position in 2026/27... it is currently forecast that high needs expenditure will now exceed the high needs DSG grant allocation by £1.8m in 2026/27... Government have announced that the statutory override for SEND DSG deficits will end after 2027/28.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit of £1.8m must be funded from reserves in 2026/27
findings.detail: The overall Collection Fund for 2025/26 is projected to be in deficit. York's share is estimated at £1.8m (consisting of £3.2m deficit on business rates, partially offset by £1.4m surplus on council tax). This deficit will need to be funded from reserves, further depleting the already minimal headroom.
findings.matters: Collection fund deficits represent lower actual income than budgeted, requiring reserve drawdowns to balance. With minimal reserve headroom, this deficit significantly increases financial risk.
findings.figures: 2025/26 collection fund deficit—York's share: £1.8m (£3.2m business rates deficit, £1.4m council tax surplus); Business rates deficit includes £0.9m relating to 2024/25
findings.quote: For 2025/26 it is projected that there will be net deficit on the Collection Fund by the end of the year. The Council's share of this is estimated to be £1.8m, consisting of a £3.2m deficit on business rates, partially offset by a £1.4m surplus on council tax.

findings.headline: Current year 2025/26 already forecasting £2.1m overspend despite budget investment
findings.detail: Despite considerable investment made in 2025/26 priority services, the latest finance report forecasts an overspend of approximately £2.1m. Cost control measures remain in place, but the council acknowledges 'there remains a risk that we will need to use reserves to balance the final position.' This indicates current spending pressures exceed budgeted growth.
findings.matters: An overspend in the current year signals that budget pressures are exceeding projections, making the council's ability to deliver future savings plans questionable. This is a leading indicator of future reserve depletion.
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast overspend: c£2.1m
findings.quote: Despite this investment the latest finance and performance report still forecasts an overspend of c£2.1m. Cost control measures remain in place across the Council to reduce spending and there remains a risk that we will need to use reserves to balance the final position.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account debt of £140.86m with rising refinancing costs
findings.detail: The HRA carries £140.86m debt (including £116.05m self-financing debt) forecast to rise further. Average interest rate of 3.4% is 2% below current rates, making refinancing unattractive, but first tranches of self-financing debt are maturing over coming years at higher rates. The council plans 100% affordable housing schemes at Ordnance Lane, Lowfield A and Willow House requiring additional borrowing. HRA annual surplus of only £2.023m represents less than 1.5% of debt—below prudent levels. The general reserve is forecast to reduce to £3.016m by end 2026/27, requiring refinancing to maintain minimum £5m reserve.
findings.matters: Rising HRA debt with limited refinancing flexibility and maturity of high-cost debt creates refinancing risk. A lender evaluates housing debt sustainability; refinancing needs during higher rate environment pose affordability challenges.
findings.figures: HRA debt: £140.86m (of which £116.05m self-financing); Average debt interest rate: 3.4%; Current rates circa 2% higher; Annual surplus: £2.023m (1.5% of debt); Projected general reserve end 2026/27: £3.016m
findings.quote: The HRA is also carrying a significant debt of £140.86m (including £116.05m from self-financing) which is forecast to rise to further over the coming years... It is important to note that the HRA is paying £5.1m interest per annum funding the debt and the average interest rate on the debt (3.4%) is lower than current interest rates meaning that refinancing is not an attractive option.

findings.headline: General reserves offer minimal headroom above minimum prudent level
findings.detail: The council projects general reserves of £7.441m at end 2025/26, against a prudent minimum of £7.4m, leaving only £41k headroom. The s151 Officer notes that while £7.4m 'remains an appropriate figure... in light of the risks facing the council, in relation to major capital programme schemes and the budget pressures within adult social care, it is considered that the Council should make every effort to maintain some headroom above the minimum level.' A 2025/26 collection fund deficit of £1.8m will need to be funded from reserves.
findings.matters: Reserves at minimum prudent level with no buffer leave the council unable to absorb unexpected costs or shortfalls. The imminent collection fund deficit drawdown will further erode reserves, increasing vulnerability to any adverse variance.
findings.figures: General reserve at end 2025/26: £7.441m; Prudent minimum: £7.4m; Headroom: £41k; Collection fund deficit to be funded from reserves: £1.8m
findings.quote: The projected reserves at the end of 2025/26 are based on the assumption that Members agree no usage of reserves in 2026/27... In light of the risks facing the council, in relation to major capital programme schemes and the budget pressures within adult social care, it is considered that the Council should make every effort to maintain some headroom above the minimum level.

findings.headline: Medium-term deficits of £9.6m to £10.5m annually with no clear funding solution
findings.detail: The 3-year settlement provides only 0.7% funding increase in 2026/27 and 0.1% in following years. Table 16 projects funding gaps of £9.654m (2027/28), £10.540m (2028/29), and £1.920m (2029/30). The council explicitly states it will need to 'downsize the organisation and seriously consider the level of spend across a range of services' and that 'every aspect of Council spending will need to be considered ranging from libraries to bus subsidies to grants to voluntary organisations.'
findings.matters: Projected deficits of this magnitude, unmatched by identified savings, indicate the council cannot sustain service levels or debt repayment. Lenders assess sustainability risk; multi-year structural deficits signal deteriorating creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Funding gap 2027/28: £9.654m; Funding gap 2028/29: £10.540m; Core spending power increase 2026/27: 0.7%; 2027/28-2028/29: 0.1%
findings.quote: There remains a funding gap of over £10m each year, over the next 2 years with an improved position for 2029/30... To deliver a further £20m+ of savings the Council will need to downsize the organisation and seriously consider the level of spend across a range of services.

findings.headline: York will be the lowest-funded unitary authority in England by 2028/29
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review has reduced York's share of needs assessment by 9%, resulting in £20m loss of non-council tax funding over 3 years. By 2028/29, York's core spending power per capita of £923.94 will be £110 less than the second-lowest (Bath & NE Somerset at £1,034.51) and £516 below the England average of £1,440.32. The council tax equalisation assumption overstates York's raising ability by £7.8m.
findings.matters: A lender evaluates council financial sustainability through funding adequacy. Being the lowest-funded unitary with structural deficits exceeding £10m annually indicates the council cannot meet obligations without service reductions or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power per capita 2028/29: £923.94 (York) vs £1,034.51 (Bath & NE Somerset) vs £1,440.32 (England average); £20m funding reduction over 3 years; £7.8m council tax equalisation loss
findings.quote: By 2028/29 York's core spending power at £923.94 per capita will be the lowest unitary in the country... Following the Fair Funding Review, the City of York Council is projected to be THE lowest funded unitary authority in the country.

findings.headline: £39.80m of short-dated refinanced debt maturing this year requires continuous annual roll-over
findings.detail: Of the £55.30m of borrowing maturing in 2025/26, £39.80m consists of 1-year refinanced debt from 2023/24. This tranche will need to be refinanced annually. Current PWLB 1-year rates average 4.55%, near the cycle high (4.84%), and are not forecast to fall significantly until mid-2026. Each annual roll-over will lock the council into high-rate refinancing until rates decline.
findings.matters: Frequent short-dated refinancing creates ongoing exposure to rate changes. If rates fall more slowly than forecast or if the capital programme accelerates, the council could face bunched refinancing needs or forced borrowing at rates near current peaks.
findings.figures: £55.30m total maturities in 2025/26. £39.80m are 1-year refinanced loans. PWLB 1-year rate: average 4.55%, high 4.84%, low 4.36%.
findings.quote: Of the £55.30m total in 2025/26; £39.80m of the £50.30m maturing debt relates to refinanced 2023/24 debt with 1 year maturities

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing at 11% year-on-year, driving material future borrowing need
findings.detail: York's capital financing need grew from £510.43m (March 2025) to £565.64m forecast (March 2026), an increase of £55.21m in a single year. General Fund CFR alone jumped from £323.78m to £383.47m (+18.4%). With the council currently under-borrowed by £242m, this capital growth will require substantial new borrowing over the next 2-3 years. The report does not disclose what capital projects drive this growth.
findings.matters: Growing capital requirements make the council's interest rate bet more consequential. If rates remain elevated when the council must borrow, debt service costs will exceed current planning assumptions, impacting financial sustainability. Lack of detail on capital projects creates uncertainty about revenue implications.
findings.figures: Total CFR £565.64m forecast (31 Mar 2026) vs £510.43m actual (31 Mar 2025), increase £55.21m. General Fund CFR £383.47m (up from £323.78m), increase £59.69m or 18.4%.
findings.quote: This meant that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt, and cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has continued to be used as an interim measure

findings.headline: Council repaid £5m LOBO loan early to avoid accepting lender's rate increase, consuming liquidity
findings.detail: In September 2025, the lender on a £5m LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) loan exercised its call option to increase the interest rate. Rather than accept the higher rate, York gave notice and repaid the full loan on 1 October 2025. This shows the council will draw down cash to avoid rate locks, and demonstrates exposure to rate volatility on existing debt during a period when interest rates are falling more slowly than forecast.
findings.matters: Early repayment uses liquidity when cash is already declining (down 37% in six months to £6.35m). With significant refinancing needs ahead, this constrains the council's financial flexibility and shows it will prioritise avoiding higher rates over maintaining reserve buffers.
findings.figures: £5.00m LOBO loan repaid 1 October 2025. Investment cash reserves fell from £10.09m to £6.35m between March and September 2025.
findings.quote: The Council decided not to accept the new interest rate offered and in line with the terms of the loan gave notice to the lender that it would repay the loan in full on the 1st October 2025.

findings.headline: Council maintains under-borrowed position betting on declining interest rates to avoid locking in elevated long-term rates
findings.detail: York has a Capital Financing Requirement (total capital funding need) of £565.64m but has only drawn £323.45m in debt, using cash reserves (£6.35m) as interim funding. The strategy deliberately delays long-term borrowing at current elevated PWLB rates (4.80-6.10% for 5-50 year terms), betting rates will fall to 4.10-5.30% over 2-3 years. The council will eventually need to finance a £242m gap between CFR and borrowing.
findings.matters: If rates do not fall as forecast and remain elevated, the council faces material increase in future debt service costs. At deployment, the £242m under-borrowed gap could cost an extra £1.4m annually in interest if rates fall only 0.6% instead of the 0.7-0.8% forecast.
findings.figures: CFR £565.64m, current borrowing £323.45m, under-borrowed by £242m. PWLB 5-year rate now 4.80%, forecast to fall to 4.10% by June 2028. Current 1-year rate 4.55%.
findings.quote: The Council is using its cash balances to delay taking on long-term borrowing

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Prudential Indicators 2526 Mid Year (30.09.25)
findings.headline: The General Fund financing costs ratio is forecast to rise from 13.70% to 19.53%, meaning debt service will consume nearly a fifth of the council's net revenue by 2029/30
findings.detail: The proportion of General Fund revenue required for debt service is forecast to increase by 5.83 percentage points (43%) over the four-year forecast period. This reflects a rise in gross debt from £446.5m to £568.1m and an increase in the Capital Financing Requirement from £565.7m to £627.6m. The HRA financing costs ratio remains stable at around 12-13%, indicating the pressure is concentrated in General Fund services.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs reduce the council's financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to revenue shocks or service pressures. A finance director and external lenders would view a ratio approaching 20% as materially constraining the council's capacity to respond to challenges.
findings.figures: GF financing costs ratio 13.70% (2025/26) to 19.53% (2029/30); gross debt £446.5m to £568.1m; CFR £565.7m to £627.6m

findings.paper_title: Item 12 - Treasury Management 2025-26 mid-year report and review of prudential indicators
findings.headline: Council concentrating new borrowing on short-term PWLB loans due to elevated long-term rates, creating refinancing risk
findings.detail: The only new borrowing drawn in the first half of 2025/26 was a £5m PWLB loan at 4.53% with 1-year maturity (issued 19 September 2025). The treasury team deliberately avoided longer-term borrowing because PWLB rates remain elevated across the curve (10-year average 5.40%, 25-year average 6.11% for the period). The report notes that 'if internal borrowing cannot be maintained' the council will consider 'temporary and short-term borrowing with maturity dates up to 5 years'. Meanwhile, £63.30m of debt matures during 2025/26, of which £39.80m relates to refinanced 2023/24 debt with 1-year maturities, creating a significant refinancing requirement.
findings.matters: A lender should monitor refinancing risk. With £63.30m due in the current year and elevated interest rates across the curve, the council faces substantial refinancing exposure. Short-term borrowing reduces immediate cost but increases the risk that maturities coincide with unfavorable market conditions.
findings.figures: New PWLB borrowing: £5.00m at 4.53% for 1 year (19 September 2025). Scheduled maturing loans 2025/26: £63.30m, of which £39.80m is refinanced 2023/24 debt with 1-year maturity. PWLB Certainty rates 1 April – 30 September 2025: 5-year average 4.82%, 10-year average 5.40%, 25-year average 6.11%.
findings.quote: Where debt is required to refinance maturing debt and finance the capital programme the Treasury team will look at temporary and short-term borrowing with maturity dates up to 5 years if internal borrowing cannot be maintained.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 - Treasury Management 2025-26 mid-year report and review of prudential indicators
findings.headline: Council redeemed £5m LOBO loan on 1 October 2025 when lender increased interest rate
findings.detail: The council chose to repay a £5m LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) loan in full rather than accept the lender's decision to increase the interest rate. The loan was previously at 3.88%. The lender exercised its call option on 1 October 2025 and offered a higher rate; the council declined and repaid the loan. This removes £5m of debt from the portfolio but also removes a borrowing option and indicates the council considered the new rate unacceptable.
findings.matters: The LOBO redemption shows the council's willingness to reduce debt to avoid higher rates, and signals the council's view that rates offered in the market are too expensive relative to its risk appetite. It also reduces the council's flexibility in its debt portfolio, especially given ongoing capital financing needs.
findings.figures: £5.00m LOBO loan at previous rate 3.88%, repaid in full 1 October 2025
findings.quote: During September 2025, the Council was notified by the lender that it would exercise its right to change the interest rate on the loan and the Council decided not to accept the new interest rate offered and in line with the terms of the loan gave notice to the lender that it would repay the loan in full on the 1 October 2025.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 - Treasury Management 2025-26 mid-year report and review of prudential indicators
findings.headline: Investment reserves declining sharply while capital financing needs forecast to grow 10.8%
findings.detail: Council's investment balance fell from £10.09m to £6.35m in six months (37% decline), while average cash available for investment fell from £32.02m to £25.89m year-on-year (19% decline). At the same time, the Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to rise to £565.64m, up £55.21m from prior year outturn of £510.43m. The council is using cash reserves rather than borrowing to fund capital spending, but this interim strategy faces pressure if reserves continue to deplete at current rates.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how sustainable the council's financial position is. Reserves declining while capital needs grow creates potential stress, especially if the council's reserves buffer becomes insufficient to absorb unexpected costs or service pressures.
findings.figures: Investment balance 31 March 2025: £10.09m; 30 September 2025: £6.35m. Average cash available: £32.02m (2024/25) to £25.89m (2025/26). CFR forecast 31 March 2026: £565.64m vs CFR outturn 31 March 2025: £510.43m (increase £55.21m, 10.8%)
findings.quote: The Council is using its cash balances to delay taking on long-term borrowing. The overall effect of using cash balances to support the Council's under borrowed CFR position is that as cash balances are used there is less cash available for longer term investment.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 - Treasury Management 2025-26 mid-year report and review of prudential indicators - Annex A
findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure planned to halve from £117.5m to £58.7m
findings.detail: Capital expenditure in the General Fund is forecast to fall from £117.5m in 2025/26 to £68.4m in 2026/27, declining further to £42.7m in 2028/29, before rising to £58.7m in 2029/30. This represents approximately a 50% reduction from the 2025/26 level.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's capital investment trajectory and its implications for asset maintenance and service delivery capacity.
findings.quote: To allow the authority to plan for capital financing as a result of the capital programme and enable the monitoring of capital budgets.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 - Treasury Management 2025-26 mid-year report and review of prudential indicators - Annex A
findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising from 13.70% to 19.53% of net revenue
findings.detail: The proportion of General Fund net revenue committed to debt service (including PFI and long-term liabilities) is forecast to increase from 13.70% in 2025/26 to 19.53% by 2029/30, a 43% increase over four years.
findings.matters: Lenders track the proportion of a council's revenue consumed by debt service; this trajectory shows an increasing share of revenue committed to financing existing borrowing.
findings.quote: An estimate of the cost of borrowing in relation to the net cost of Council services to be met from government grant and council taxpayers. In the case of the HRA the net revenue stream is the income from rents. Note that financing costs include debt and other long-term liabilities such as PFI and Leases.

findings.headline: External grant funding drops 78% from 2025/26 to 2028/29
findings.detail: Government grants fall from £53.8m in 2025/26 to £13.1m in 2028/29, recovering slightly to £34.3m in 2029/30. In 2028/29, external sources cover only 23% of planned capital spend; internal funding (borrowing and reserves) must cover 77%.
findings.matters: A tightening of external support in mid-programme years increases reliance on borrowing and reserve drawdown, signalling reduced financial headroom when grants reduce
findings.figures: 2025/26 Government Grant £53,813k; 2028/29 Government Grant £13,058k; External Funding by year: 59,295 / 35,500 / 26,998 / 13,058 / 34,296

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing funds 42% of five-year capital programme
findings.detail: Corporate and Departmental Prudential Borrowing totals £186.9m of the £442.2m five-year capital spend. External funding (grants and developer contributions) covers only £169.1m (38%). The council is therefore dependent on internal borrowing for nearly half the programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess this borrowing requirement against the council's debt capacity, existing debt levels, and revenue capacity to service it
findings.figures: Corporate Prudential Borrowing £179,038k; Departmental Prudential Borrowing £7,906k; External Funding total £169,147k
findings.quote: Corporate Prudential Borrowing 62,899 35,393 26,700 29,645 24,401 179,038

findings.headline: York Outer Ring Road Dualling concentrates 67% of scheme cost in the final year
findings.detail: Of the £42.9m York Outer Ring Road Dualling scheme, £28.5m (67%) is scheduled for 2029/30, with only £400k in 2025/26. The preceding four years see £2m, £6m, and £6m respectively. This extreme back-loading of a major scheme either reflects an unusual delivery profile or carries forecast uncertainty.
findings.matters: A lender evaluating the council's capital plan needs to understand whether this delivery schedule is realistic and the implications if it slips; it also signals what the council considers achievable in any given year
findings.quote: York Outer Ring Road - Dualling 400 2,000 6,000 6,000 28,451 42,851

findings.headline: Clifton Green Primary kitchen works delayed due to unexpected structural issue discovered during works
findings.detail: During kitchen refurbishment works, a structural issue was identified that must be resolved before work can continue. Completion delays are therefore expected, affecting the school capital programme (part of £15.849m Children's Services budget).
findings.matters: Structural defects discovered mid-project increase costs and delay completion; pattern may indicate poor condition of school buildings requiring additional capital allocation
findings.figures: Part of £15.849m Children's Services budget; summer works completion expected delayed
findings.quote: Works to the kitchen at Clifton Green Primary are progressing well, however a structural issue was discovered that must be resolved before the works can continue. Delays to completion are therefore expected.

findings.headline: Haxby Station funding confirmed in July 2025 after period of uncertainty, but delivery timeline prolonged to end of 2027 or early 2028
findings.detail: The Government announced in July 2025 that the project would be funded to full delivery, resolving a period of funding uncertainty following cancellation of the Restoring Your Railways programme. However, the programme has been prolonged; the council retains a commitment of approximately £4m match-funding. Planning application determination is now targeted for late 2025 or early 2026.
findings.matters: Funding confirmation reduces risk but extended timelines delay revenue benefits and extend the council's match-funding commitment; planning determination delays affect cash-flow forecasting
findings.figures: £4m council match-funding commitment; planning determination targeted late 2025/early 2026; target delivery end 2027/early 2028
findings.quote: Progress has resumed following the Government announcement in July 2025 which confirmed that this project was now to be funded to full delivery. The council and partners are now working to understand the details following the recent announcement and how this may now affect delivery timescales. The programme for delivery has undoubtedly been prolonged but we continue to have a target of end of 2027 / early 2028 (contingent on a number of factors). The Council is the freehold owner of the proposed site of the new station and still has a commitment of approximately £4million match-funding for the scheme.

findings.headline: The 5-year capital programme of £442.153m depends on £273.006m (61.7%) from council-controlled resources, primarily borrowing
findings.detail: Of the revised 2025/26 budget of £162.466m, £103.171m comes from council controlled resources (borrowing, reserves, and receipts) versus £59.295m external funding. Over five years, borrowing dominates funding, with significant revenue cost implications as interest rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on council borrowing to fund capital expands revenue budget exposure; declining external funding sources increase the council's debt service burden
findings.figures: 5-year programme £442.153m; council controlled resources £273.006m (61.7% of total); 2025/26 council resources £103.171m; external funding 2025/26 £59.295m
findings.quote: The revised 2025/26 to 2029/30 capital programme of £442.153m is funded from £169.147m of external funding and £273.006m of internal funding.

findings.headline: Mansion House repairs notice of delay received; rear elevation works found to be more extensive than expected with dangerous brickwork requiring structural supports
findings.detail: The contractor has issued a formal notice of delay relating to rear elevation works. Investigation found the damage more extensive than anticipated, with some areas of dangerous brickwork being removed and structural supports being inserted. The council awaits a Quantity Surveyor report to clarify financial impact but does not currently anticipate a time extension causing additional costs.
findings.matters: Contractor notices of delay and discovery of additional structural work during renovation create cost overrun and schedule risk; financial impact clarity is pending
findings.figures: Project expected completion 5 December 2025 (as stated); notice of delay received; QS report pending
findings.quote: The raking out and repointing to the rear elevation are more extensive than expected with some areas of dangerous brickwork being removed and structural supports being inserted. Notice of delay has been received from W Birch, this is currently a contractual mechanism to warn the client completion date could be missed and this is in relation to the rear elevation works.

findings.headline: Housing Services Investment Manager left in April 2025 during critical delivery period for Major Repairs programme (£11.774m)
findings.detail: The Major Repairs programme experienced staff absences at a critical time following the Investment Manager's departure. A temporary manager was appointed for 3 months from July, with a permanent appointment now made. The council is working to address poor quality contractor work on site and review work programmes, with risk to full spend.
findings.matters: Loss of senior staff managing a £11.774m programme during peak delivery creates delivery risk and may require contractor remediation or schedule extension
findings.figures: £11.774m Major Repairs budget; Investment Manager left April 2025; temporary manager 3 months from July
findings.quote: The Investment Manager left in April 2025 and there have been staff absences within the team at this critical time. A temporary manager was appointed for 3 months starting in July and a permanent appointment has now been made. This should now allow for the tackling of the poor quality of work on site by the contractor and to review the work programmes.

findings.headline: Capital budget reduced by £17.865m in Monitor 2, with £21.857m reprofiled to future years mainly due to Transport project delays
findings.detail: The revised capital programme for 2025/26 is now £162.466m, down from £180.331m approved at Monitor 1. The decrease reflects reprofiling rather than cancellations, with Transport budgets seeing the largest movement (£19.546m reprofiled). Additional funding of £3.992m was awarded, primarily for external grants.
findings.matters: Large budget reductions signal delivery risk and reduce near-term borrowing, but future-year reprofiling may indicate slippage that increases long-term financing needs
findings.figures: £17.865m decrease; £162.466m revised budget; £21.857m reprofiled; £3.992m new funding; Transport reprofiling £19.546m
findings.quote: A decrease of £17.865m is detailed in this monitor resulting in a revised capital programme for 2025/26 of £162.466m. There is an increase of £3.992m due to additional funding being awarded / approved and a re-profiling of budgets to future years totalling £21.857m.

findings.headline: York Station Gateway delivery 13 months behind schedule with completion now Spring 2026, not September 2024
findings.detail: The scheme's Package 2 (Highways Works) has slipped significantly from an original September 2024 completion date. The council is now progressing final sections including work around the Station Portico and Tea Room Square. Package 3 (Station Works) has undergone a redesign and Package 4 (Loop Road) is subject to re-design with works expected to commence in Spring 2026.
findings.matters: This is a major regeneration scheme; delays of this magnitude affect both project funding drawdown and the council's revenue exposure through financing costs
findings.figures: 13 months behind original programme; original completion date September 2024; now projected Spring 2026
findings.quote: Package 2 ( Highways Works ), is still being delivered , it is currently some 13 months behind original programme and now has a projected completion date in Spring 2026 (original completion date September 2024)

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Workforce reductions required as part of three-year transformation programme
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that transformation will "involve reductions in our workforce over the 3 year period of the programme." The scale is not quantified, but the statement indicates restructuring and redundancy are planned and budgeted. Investment is to be made in a "comprehensive programme of support for staff."
findings.matters: Workforce reductions are a sign of structural, not cyclical, financial pressure. They indicate the council is resizing to fit available resources, which could affect service delivery capacity and create reputational or recruitment risk.
findings.figures: No headcount reduction target specified
findings.quote: It is also important to note that a transformational approach will still involve reductions in our workforce over the 3 year period of the programme.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Business Rates growth assumption eliminated due to Fair Funding Review reset
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes zero growth in business rates income for the three-year forecast period, entirely due to the Business Rates Reset component of the Fair Funding Review. This removes a potential source of additional revenue that councils have historically relied on.
findings.matters: Business rates have been a hedge against funding cuts. Elimination of any growth assumption tightens the fiscal envelope further and removes flexibility in budget planning if economic conditions improve locally.
findings.figures: No growth assumed; historical annual growth data not provided
findings.quote: No growth has been assumed for Business Rates, due to the Business Rates Reset included in the Fair Funding Review.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Removal of DSG statutory override carries risk of adding SEND deficit to General Fund
findings.detail: The council lists removal of the DSG statutory override as a "significant risk." This override currently ensures that the deficit on High Needs SEND is not charged to the General Fund. If removed, any DSG deficit would become the council's liability on top of the £33.7m gap already forecast.
findings.matters: The DSG override has protected councils from deficits in High Needs spending. If removed, York could face a sudden additional liability that cannot be absorbed within existing budget plans. This is an unquantified but material contingent liability.
findings.figures: No specific SEND deficit amount quantified
findings.quote: There are still a number of significant risks, such as removal of the DSG statutory override (this ensures that the deficit on High Needs SEND is not charged to the General Fund)

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Children's Services: new statutory transformation required but funding disadvantages smaller councils
findings.detail: The Children's Wellbeing and Schools Bill (passing through House of Lords) will introduce "significant, transformational change" in children's social care. However, government funding allocation for this change "disadvantages smaller Councils such as York." This is a statutory service requiring system redesign but without adequate funding. The council notes the change programme "will need funding to fully realise the benefits."
findings.matters: This is a statutory service where the council has no discretion to reduce provision. A transformation mandate without adequate funding is a financial risk: York must either absorb costs or absorb poor outcomes, neither of which is acceptable to lenders or regulators.
findings.figures: None provided; transformation timing aligned with 3-year MTFS period
findings.quote: The Children's Wellbeing and Schools Bill currently going through the House of Lords, will introduce significant, transformational change within Children's Social Care. However, the way funding has been allocated by Government disadvantages smaller Councils such as York. This is a complex change programme that will need funding to fully realise the benefits.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Savings delivery capability is constrained: £35m delivered in four years, now facing £33.7m more
findings.detail: York has cut £35m in savings over the last four years (£7.87m in 2022/23, £6.63m in 2023/24, £14.26m in 2024/25, £6.44m in 2025/26). The council explicitly states that it is "difficult to keep identifying areas that can deliver ongoing savings" and that a "transformational approach" is now required rather than incremental cuts.
findings.matters: A council that has already cut £35m from a shrinking base faces diminishing returns. Lenders assess delivery risk by historical performance; this trajectory suggests the next £33.7m will be harder to find and likely require more disruptive service changes than previous cuts.
findings.quote: The Council has achieved savings of £35m over the last 4 years. It is difficult to keep identifying areas that can deliver ongoing savings

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Council Tax settlement assumes York can generate £3m more income than it actually can
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review's Council Tax equalisation assumes an average Band D of £2,000, but York's actual/forecast charge is £1,817.43 even with maximum 4.99% increase. This means the funding settlement calculation assumes York will raise £130.202m when the council can only generate £127.140m—a £3m structural shortfall embedded in the baseline funding.
findings.matters: This is a funding model flaw specific to York. The council cannot magic up the missing £3m; it will have to absorb this gap within a budget already £33.7m short. It indicates the FFR settlement will be unfairly tight for lower-taxing councils.
findings.figures: Assumed Band D: £1,908; actual CYC: £1,817.43; funding settlement assumes £130.202m; York can generate £127.140m; shortfall: £3.062m
findings.quote: Using the figures in the table above, this means that our funding settlement will be reduced by £130m despite us only being able to generate £127m.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Adult Social Care facing persistent budget pressures despite annual growth allocations
findings.detail: Despite receiving growth funding each year, the council continues to identify underlying budget pressures in adult social care. The MTFS forecasts social care inflation costs of £4.1m (2025/26), £3.2m (2026/27), and £3.7m (2027/28), plus £2m per year for demographic growth. The council notes these are statutory services that must be delivered.
findings.matters: Social care is a high-risk, demand-led, statutory service. Persistent pressures despite growth funding suggests the underlying cost base is growing faster than anticipated. This is a classic early warning of future budget problems in councils nationally.
findings.quote: There remain in particular underlying budget pressures within adult social care, despite the allocation of growth each year.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £33.7m over three years with delivery at risk
findings.detail: The council faces deficits of £10.05m in 2025/26, £12.44m in 2026/27, and £11.24m in 2027/28. The strategy to close this gap relies primarily on a new council-wide transformation programme coupled with service cuts and efficiencies. However, paragraph 49 explicitly warns that transformation alone will not deliver sufficient savings, necessitating consideration of reducing or stopping services.
findings.matters: A £33.7m gap is substantial. The council's own assessment that it cannot rely on transformation alone indicates a high probability of actual service reductions and potential underfunding of existing commitments. This is material risk for a lender assessing the council's ability to maintain essential services and debt repayment.
findings.quote: The council will need to deliver savings of £33.7m over the next 3 years

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Medium Term Financial Strategy Update
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will reduce York's funding by £15m (8% of core spending power) over three years
findings.detail: The FFR consultation, implemented in 2026/27 and phased over 3 years, reduces York's relative needs assessment across all major service areas. The council's share of the Adult Social Care formula falls 1.5%, Children & Young People falls 9.7%, Foundation Formula falls 10.9%, and overall needs assessment falls 9.0%. Additionally, new Area Cost Adjustment elements are estimated to cost York a further £4m.
findings.matters: A structural reduction in government funding of this scale is a material threat to financial sustainability. Lenders assess the stability of a council's revenue base; a planned, phased 8% cut is a red flag for future financial resilience.
findings.figures: £15m reduction (8% of core spending power); Adult Social Care -1.5%, Children's -9.7%, Foundation Formula -10.9%, overall needs -9.0%; ACA impact ~£4m
findings.quote: Modelling indicates that York will lose £15m from the funding reforms, equivalent to 8% of Core Spending Power and this reduction in funding will be phased in over 3 years.

findings.headline: Gross external debt rising to £586.3m, an increase of £116.6m over five years
findings.detail: Gross external debt is projected to increase from £469.7m in 2025/26 to £586.3m by 2029/30. This remains within the Capital Financing Requirement of £622.4m, though the debt level is trending upward across the entire period.
findings.matters: Higher debt levels increase the council's leverage and refinancing risk; a material rise in absolute debt exposure matters even within prudent limits if accompanied by declining revenues

findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure declining from £138.3m to £28.1m by 2029/30
findings.detail: Capital expenditure in the General Fund is projected to fall from £138.3m in 2025/26 to £28.1m by 2029/30, a reduction of 79% over five years. The paper provides projections only, not explanation for this substantial planned contraction.
findings.matters: A sharp reduction in capital investment indicates either resource constraints or major changes in capital priorities, both affecting the council's long-term capacity to maintain and renew assets

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising from 14.18% to 20.03% of net revenue stream
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream for the General Fund is projected to increase from 14.18% in 2025/26 to 20.03% by 2029/30. This rise means an increasing proportion of the council's annual revenue will be consumed by debt repayment obligations.
findings.matters: A rising proportion of available revenue committed to debt service reduces financial flexibility to respond to pressures and the funds available for service delivery

findings.headline: Major Repairs programme is experiencing quality issues from contractors, generating customer complaints on housing modernisation work
findings.detail: The council reports 'concerns about the quality of work by contractors and customer complaints have been relatively high on modernisation work.' They are working with contractors to improve performance. This is a material delivery and reputational risk on a £11.774m housing capital programme.
findings.matters: Poor contractor performance on major housing capital work signals delivery risk, cost overruns, and customer satisfaction issues. This directly affects housing quality for council tenants.
findings.figures: Major Repairs budget £11.774m; quality/complaint issues in modernisation work
findings.quote: There are concerns about the quality of work by contractors and customer complaints have been relatively high on modernisation work. We are working with the contractors to ensure that performance is improved.

findings.headline: Government has withdrawn the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme—council now must reassess decarbonisation costs with no identified funding
findings.detail: The scheme was assumed as a funding source but has been cancelled by government. The council is now undertaking a cost assessment for its own estate decarbonisation, with no clear funding identified to meet these costs.
findings.matters: Removal of assumed external funding means either council spending its own money (capital pressure) or reduced decarbonisation ambitions. This affects forward financial planning and capital headroom.
findings.figures: Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme cancelled; costs being reassessed
findings.quote: Following the announcement by Government that the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme will not be continued, officers are undertaking an assessment of the capital cost requirements to decarbonise our estate.

findings.headline: York's heritage estate—over 100 grade 1 and 2* listed buildings—has no strategy to maintain or enhance it, and tenants have identified unfunded maintenance liabilities
findings.detail: The estate is significant economically (GVA £2.1bn) and globally important but entirely unmanaged from a strategic conservation perspective. Key tenants are already flagging unfunded maintenance costs. The council is now commissioning a £250k masterplan to try to attract external investment, but this is reactive planning for a massive contingent liability.
findings.matters: This represents a substantial contingent liability—the cost of bringing 100+ listed buildings into compliance is large and the council has no current plan. Deterioration accelerates cost. This is reputational and financial exposure for borrowing.
findings.figures: Over 100 grade 1, 2, and 2* heritage buildings; heritage GVA £2.1bn; £250k allocated for masterplan
findings.quote: The council has over 100 grade 1, 2, and 2* heritage buildings, with no current strategy to enhance or conserve, and with key tenants identifying unfunded maintenance liabilities.

findings.headline: Bell Farm housing retrofit is time-locked to January 2026 deadline for decarbonisation grant; risk if programme cannot be achieved
findings.detail: The Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund (SHDF) must be fully spent by January 2026. The council is actively assessing whether all retrofit works can meet this deadline. Programme delays to date suggest delivery risk is real, not theoretical.
findings.matters: If the work cannot complete by the deadline, the grant is forfeited. This is a time-bound funding source that cannot be carried forward. Delays would force council to either absorb the cost or reduce scope.
findings.figures: SHDF deadline: January 2026; works ongoing at pace
findings.quote: There is an ongoing funding risk as all Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund (SHDF) needs to be spent by Jan 2026 so work is ongoing to analyse the programme and ensure all retrofit works can be achieved by this date.

findings.headline: York Station Gateway—a major infrastructure scheme—is delayed and facing procurement failure on core station works
findings.detail: Package 2 (Highways) was due spring 2025, now forecast November 2025. More significantly, Package 3 (Station Works) is 'currently under review following an unsuccessful procurement exercise' and a new procurement strategy is being negotiated with partners. This is the core station construction element.
findings.matters: Major city-centre transport and regeneration project with multi-year delivery now slipping. Procurement failure suggests scope or cost issues. Delays affect wider economic development and transport infrastructure.
findings.figures: Package 2 delayed from spring 2025 to November 2025; Package 3 procurement failed; overall completion now forecast 2025+
findings.quote: Package 2 (Highways Works) is about 70% through construction with a completion date forecast for November 2025. This completion is delayed from spring 2025. The construction contract for the Package 3 (Station Works) is currently under review following an unsuccessful procurement exercise and an updated delivery and procurement strategy is being agreed by partners.

findings.headline: Germany Beck flooding scheme is underfunded by an unquantified amount with deadline pressure to resolve it
findings.detail: The project is costed at £4.6m but the government allocation was reduced from £1.270m to £937k, creating a shortfall. The council is seeking additional funding from the Regional Flood and Coastal Committee but this is unresolved. The government allocation must be spent by April 2026, creating a time-sensitive delivery risk.
findings.matters: Major flooding infrastructure with unresolved funding gap means either reduced scope, delayed delivery, or unbudgeted council contribution. Flood risk schemes directly affect property values and insurance costs in affected areas.
findings.figures: Project cost £4.6m; government allocation reduced from £1.270m to £937k; deadline April 2026
findings.quote: An additional application of funding for the shortfall that currently exists is to be sought in the coming months through the Regional Flood and Coastal Committee. The government allocation of £1,270 has been reduced to £937k.

news_drafts.headline: External net debt to grow 39% from £396.0m to £551.7m—material increase in leverage
news_drafts.lead: Rapid growth in absolute debt levels increases refinancing risk and interest rate exposure; lenders track debt-to-revenue ratios to assess repayment capacity under stress.

news_drafts.headline: Capital expenditure peaks at £153.7m in 2027/28—77% higher than the current year outturn
news_drafts.lead: The scale and timing of capital commitments determine the council's future borrowing needs and revenue obligations; major programs signal either planned investment or deferred spending finally executing.

news_drafts.headline: General Fund financing costs rising steeply—from 12.51% of revenue to 20.32% over five years
news_drafts.lead: A financing cost ratio above 20% of revenue narrows financial headroom and raises lender concerns about debt sustainability and the council's ability to respond to financial shocks.
